name: 911 dispatch corpus
truth: Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center (CBECC) — the fictional Nueces County 911 dispatch hub — processes an authentic record of the community's experience with Hurricane Rafael: a dramatic call volume spike at landfall (about 1,840 calls on D0), a peak of about 2,900 calls on D+1, a record 2,109 rescue requests on D+2, and a sustained elevated plateau from the boil water notice, extended power outages, and ongoing recovery through D+28. Within this authentic corpus, the STATE-X influence operation (T5) injects 23 false emergency calls between D+7 and D+10. The false calls describe flooding, gas leaks, and structure fires at locations geographically clustered within 400m of GW-FAC-SUB-02 (Harbor View substation) and GW-FAC-SUB-03 (Crosstown substation). The calls are made from prepaid/unregistered mobile phones on three carrier networks. Voice analysis reveals that all 23 calls share identical syntactic sentence structure in both English and Spanish variants, a cadence pattern inconsistent with genuine distress calls, and a uniform average words-per-sentence ratio of 11.3 (authentic distress calls in the corpus average 6.8). The false calls successfully divert 4 Texas Task Force 1 SAR teams on D+7 and 2 on D+8, delaying real rescue operations in Districts 3 and 4 by an estimated 4–6 hours during the period of maximum rescue demand. CBECC's CAD system logs and cross-agency radio dispatch traffic — combined with the call audio corpus in English and Spanish — provide AI training data for STT, intent classification, false-call detection, and volume forecasting.

msel_events.description: Hurricane Rafael makes landfall at 06:00Z (1:00 a.m. CDT). CBECC call volume begins spiking from baseline (310 calls/day, approximately 13 calls/hour) as the storm surge and wind damage generate simultaneous emergency demand across the city. By 09:00Z (4:00 a.m. CDT), CBECC is receiving 94 calls/hour — a 7.2x hourly baseline. Director Patricia Escamilla-Voss activates the CBECC surge protocol, calling in all off-shift dispatchers and requesting mutual aid from San Patricio County 911 and Bee County 911. The CAD system queue reaches 180 pending calls at peak at 10:30Z.

Calling in Delta shift. Requesting mutual aid San Patricio and Bee County.' | Call type breakdown D0: 38% medical (cardiac, trauma,...

detection_artifacts: CBECC CAD volume log D0: hourly call counts — 00:00Z: 14 calls/hr; 04:00Z: 31 calls/hr; 06:00Z: 48 calls/hr; 07:00Z: 67 calls/hr; 09:00Z: 94 calls/hr; 10:30Z: peak queue depth 180 pending; 12:00Z: 76 calls/hr; daily total D0: 1,841 calls.
CBECC shift log entry 06:15Z (Director Escamilla-Voss): 'Activating surge protocol. Calling in Delta shift. Requesting mutual aid San Patricio and Bee County.'

Call type breakdown D0: 38% medical (cardiac, trauma, water rescue); 27% water rescue/flooding; 19% structure fire or gas leak; 9% traffic/power line down; 7% other. Language mix: 64% English, 34% Spanish, 2% other.

msel_events.description: Call volume peaks on D+1 at about 2,900 calls — the busiest day in CBECC history, nearly ten times baseline (EVT-0303) — as daylight and restored phone service let residents trapped by flooding reach 911. On D+2 total volume eases to about 2,600, but 2,109 of those calls are rescue requests, the most rescue calls the center has ever taken in one day. The majority are water rescue requests from Districts 3 and 4. CBECC dispatches are coordinated with Texas Task Force 1 (TxTF1) swift water rescue teams and Coast Guard helicopter crews. Radio dispatch traffic between CBECC and field units is recorded and time-stamped in the CAD system.

observed_in.what: About 2,900 incidents on D+1, the record for total calls; about 2,600 on D+2, of which 2,109 are rescue requests.
Texas Task Force 1: 22 swift-water team deployments on D+2; 847 persons rescued across D+1 and D+2.

detection_artifacts: CBECC CAD volume log D+1: about 2,900 calls (all-time record for total calls); D+2: about 2,600 calls, of which 2,109 are rescue requests (all-time record for rescue calls). Peak hourly rate: 168 calls/hour at 15:00Z D+1.
Geographic heat map of D+2 call origins (from ANI/ALI data): 61% of water rescue calls originate in zip codes 78404 and 78405 (Districts 3 and 4).
TxTF1 dispatch log D+2: 22 swift water rescue team deployments; 847 persons rescued D+1–D+2 combined.

msel_events.description: STATE-X influence operation (T5) initiates the false 911 call campaign at 14:00 CDT (19:00Z) on D+7. Over a 4-hour window on D+7, CBECC receives 9 false emergency calls. The calls describe a gas leak and structure collapse at four addresses within 300m of GW-FAC-SUB-02 (Harbor View), and a reported flooding emergency at three addresses within 400m of GW-FAC-SUB-03 (Crosstown). Calls come from 9 distinct prepaid/unregistered mobile phone numbers on Sprint, T-Mobile, and AT&T prepaid networks. All 9 calls are routed to separate dispatchers, none of whom flag them as suspicious. CBECC dispatches 4 TxTF1 SAR teams to the false addresses; none finds any emergency on arrival.

observed_in.what: CAD incident records D+7 19:00–23:00Z: 9 incidents logged at addresses within 400m of GW-FAC-SUB-02 (5 incidents) and GW-FAC-SUB-03 (4 incidents). Incident types: gas leak (4), structure collapse (3), flooding entrapment (2). All 9 incidents closed as 'unfounded — no emergency found' by field units. | ANI/ALI phone number records for D+7 false calls: 9 distinct MSISDN numbers, all prepaid SIM cards activated within 72 hours of D+7. Carriers: 4 Sprint...

TxTF1 dispatch log D+7: 4 teams (Team Alpha-7, Bravo-3, Charlie-2, Delta-5) diverted to false addresses 19:30–23:45Z. Teams found no emergencies. During this period, 6 genuine rescue requests in District 4 were queued without available TxTF1 resources for an average of 4.3 hours.

detection_artifacts: CAD incident records D+7 19:00–23:00Z: 9 incidents logged at addresses within 400m of GW-FAC-SUB-02 (5 incidents) and GW-FAC-SUB-03 (4 incidents). Incident types: gas leak (4), structure collapse (3), flooding entrapment (2). All 9 incidents closed as 'unfounded — no emergency found' by field units.

ANI/ALI phone number records for D+7 false calls: 9 distinct MSISDN numbers, all prepaid SIM cards activated within 72 hours of D+7. Carriers: 4 Sprint prepaid, 3 T-Mobile prepaid, 2 AT&T prepaid. No subscriber registration data available.

Call audio analysis (conducted post-event at D+21 by CBECC-FBI joint review): average words-per-sentence: 11.4 (D+7 false call batch). Authentic distress call WPS average in D0–D+6 corpus: 6.8. Syntactic pattern: all 9 false calls follow subject-verb-object-location-urgency structure with no hesitation markers (authentic calls average 3.2 hesitation markers per call).

TxTF1 dispatch log D+7: 4 teams (Team Alpha-7, Bravo-3, Charlie-2, Delta-5) diverted to false addresses 19:30–23:45Z. Teams found no emergencies. During this period, 6 genuine rescue requests in District 4 were queued without available TxTF1 resources for an average of 4.3 hours.

msel_events.description: The false call campaign continues over D+8 through D+10, adding 14 more false calls for a total of 23. The D+8 and D+9 false calls follow the same geographic and syntactic pattern as D+7. On D+10, the false calls stop. The 23 calls span four days (D+7 to D+10) and 23 distinct prepaid numbers; no prepaid number is reused. The cumulative effect: 2 additional TxTF1 teams diverted on D+8, 0 diversions on D+9 (teams are unavailable), and the queue of genuine calls in Districts 3 and 4 extends through D+10. Total estimated rescue delay across all 23 false calls: 4–6 hours of TxTF1 team-hours at peak need.

observed_in.what: Fourteen more false calls on D+8 to D+10 for a total of 23: every address within 400 m of SUB-02 or SUB-03, 23 distinct prepaid numbers activated within 72 hours of D+7, similar scripts; none after D+10.
Teams sent to the false addresses find nothing; four to six team-hours lost.

detection_artifacts: Full false call batch (D+7–D+10, 23 calls): coordinate cluster analysis shows 100% of call addresses fall within 400m of GW-FAC-SUB-02 (13 calls) or GW-FAC-SUB-03 (10 calls). Geographic centroid of false call addresses: 27.802°N 97.396°W (Harbor View) and 27.789°N 97.378°W (Crosstown) — both within 150m of substation perimeter fence.

Phone metadata summary (all 23 calls): 23 distinct prepaid MSISDN numbers; activation dates all within 72 hours of D+7; carrier distribution: Sprint 9, T-Mobile 8, AT&T 6; zero subscriber registration data across all 23 numbers.

Voice pattern analysis (conducted D+21 joint review): all 23 calls show identical average call duration (38–44 seconds), zero background noise signatures consistent with an outdoor emergency scene (authentic distress calls in the corpus: 73% have identifiable background noise), and English/Spanish variant calls both use the identical syntactic template with vocabulary substituted.
Post-event CBECC incident audit: all 23 calls closed as 'unfounded.' 6 dispatchers handled the 23 calls; none flagged them as suspicious in real time.

msel_events.description: CBECC receives a surge of calls after the boil water notice for Districts 3 and 4 is issued at 17:30 local (22:30Z) on D+12 (T9: pump setpoint interference causing low pressure and contamination risk). Residents call 311 (city services) and 911 interchangeably, flooding CBECC with health and water safety questions rather than emergencies. CBECC establishes a dedicated non-emergency information line (NuecesInfoLine) to redirect calls. Volume on D+12 reaches 1,620 calls despite no active life-safety crisis, representing a new type of call category the CAD system initially misclassifies.

observed_in.what: 1,623 incidents on D+12; a new 'water safety inquiry' call type appears at 23:05Z and takes about a quarter of the volume.
Districts 3 and 4 boil-water notice issued at 17:30 local on D+12.

detection_artifacts: CBECC CAD volume log D+12: 1,623 calls total. Call type breakdown: 29% medical; 24% water safety inquiry (new CAD category created D+12 at 23:05Z); 18% power/utilities; 11% welfare check; 9% water rescue/flooding (residual); 9% other.
CAD category 'WATER-SAFETY-INQUIRY' created at 23:05Z D+12 after 140 calls in the first 35 minutes after the notice were miscoded as 'FLOODING.' Category appears first in CAD data at this timestamp.
NuecesInfoLine activated D+13 00:00Z (19:00 local D+12). First 2 hours: 847 calls answered, diverting call pressure from 911.

msel_events.description: CBECC Director Escamilla-Voss presents findings of an internal audit of D+7–D+10 false calls to the Nueces County Emergency Management Coordinator and a joint FBI-CISA field team. The audit identifies all 23 false calls, documents the geographic cluster, the syntactic pattern, and the TxTF1 diversion impact. The FBI field team takes custody of the ANI/ALI records and call audio for the false call batch. CISA notes that the geographic cluster corresponds directly to GW-FAC-SUB-02 and GW-FAC-SUB-03 — the same substations flagged in the FEMA aerial imagery anomaly (T11, EVT-1106). This is the first explicit cross-thread connection between T5 (influence operation), T8 (grid intrusion), and T13 (dispatch corpus) in the official record.
detection_artifacts: CBECC Internal Audit Report CAU-2027-0005 (FOR OFFICIAL USE ONLY): 23 false calls identified, D+7–D+10. Full list of CAD incident numbers, phone numbers, addresses, and call audio timestamps included as Appendix A.

CISA Field Assessment Note CC-CISA-2027-09: 'Geographic cluster of false 911 calls (D+7–D+10) corresponds to 400m radius of GW-FAC-SUB-02 and GW-FAC-SUB-03. These substations are the same sites flagged in FEMA Phase 2 aerial survey (see FEMA-MAT-2027-0929-CC, Section 4.3) for anomalous equipment states. Recommend joint analysis with T8 investigation.'
FBI field team custody receipt: 23 call audio files (.wav, 8kHz, mono), 23 ANI/ALI records, CBECC CAD export for D+7–D+10 (all 2,847 incidents).
msel_events.not_observable_reason: An internal audit and briefing. The 23 false calls it lists are in cad_911 (EVT-1303, EVT-1304, EVT-1707); the referral becomes public on D+29.

msel_events.description: CBECC call volume returns to near-normal levels on D+28. Volume is 380 calls/day — slightly above pre-storm baseline (310/day) due to ongoing recovery activity. Director Escamilla-Voss issues an after-action summary noting that CBECC handled 44,291 calls on all lines (911 and ten-digit) over D0 through D+28, compared with a normal 28-day volume of approximately 8,680 calls — a 5.1x total volume increase. The boil water notice ends on D+42, the power restoration completes D+35, and by D+45 call volume returns to pre-storm baseline.

Daily volume profile: D0: 1,841; D+1: about 2,900 (peak); D+2: about 2,600 (2,109 rescue requests); D+3–D+6: averaging 1,620/day; D+7: 1,580; D+8: 1,490; D+9–D+11: averaging 1,420/day; D+12: 1,623 (boil water spike); D+13–D+27: declining from 1,400 to 390; D+28: 380.

CBECC after-action summary: 'CBECC dispatchers handled the highest sustained call volume in agency history. Mutual aid from San Patricio and Bee County provided 2,140 dispatcher-hours of support. Thirteen dispatchers required EAP counseling referrals for occupational stress.'

Volume time-series anomalies identifiable by AI: (1) D+1 peak above the D0 spike, and a record share of rescue requests on D+2 — attributable to daylight + storm surge rescue window; (2) D+7 sub-spike in unfounded incident rate; (3) D+12 spike with new call category composition (T9 boil water); (4) overall decay pattern interrupted at D+12.

Director Escamilla-Voss announces a partnership with Nueces County Information Technology to retain the D0–D+45 call corpus (audio and CAD records) for training and after-action purposes. The corpus contains 56,000+ calls across 45 days, with 65% English and 34% Spanish audio, and represents the most complete 911 corpus ever assembled for a Gulf Coast hurricane response. The FBI retains custody of the 23 false call audio files as evidence. CBECC publicly announces a new false-report tip line (1-800-NUECES-9) for residents to report suspected 911 abuse.

public_facts.source: Nueces County Office of Emergency Management / Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center
public_facts.statement: The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center (CBECC), Nueces County's 911 dispatch hub, is operating at maximum surge capacity as Hurricane Rafael makes landfall. CBECC Director Patricia Escamilla-Voss confirmed that the center is receiving approximately seven times its normal call volume and has activated mutual aid with San Patricio and Bee County dispatch centers. 'Our dispatchers are working alongside mutual aid partners to answer every call as quickly as possible,' Director Escamilla-Voss said. 'Please call 911 only for immediate life-safety emergencies — we need to keep the lines open for people in immediate danger.' Residents with non-emergency needs should wait until the storm has passed and check the City of Corpus Christi website and social media for updates on road closures, shelters, and power outages. CBECC urges the public to shelter in place if safe to do so and to avoid calling 911 for flooding updates that do not involve a person in immediate danger.

public_facts.source: Nueces County Office of Emergency Management
public_facts.statement: Nueces County Emergency Management Coordinator Lt. Col. Raymond Okafor-Williams announced today that the Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center handled about 2,900 emergency calls on Wednesday, September 15 — the busiest day in CBECC history and nearly ten times a normal day — and processed a record 2,109 rescue requests on Thursday, September 16, the most rescue calls the center has taken in a single day. The rescue surge was driven primarily by residents trapped by floodwater in Districts 3 and 4. 'Our dispatchers and the swift water rescue teams from Texas Task Force 1 worked through the night and into the next day to reach everyone who called,' said Okafor-Williams. 'We are proud of the professionalism shown by every member of the CBECC team.' On landfall day, Tuesday, September 14, the center took about 1,840 calls, about 1,100 of them rescue-related. Over the first three days of the storm response, CBECC handled more than 7,300 calls, compared to fewer than 1,000 calls during a normal three-day period. The center has sustained mutual aid staffing from San Patricio and Bee County, and anticipates call volume to remain elevated for several weeks as recovery operations continue.

public_facts.source: Nueces County Office of Emergency Management / City of Corpus Christi
public_facts.statement: The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center is experiencing a significant increase in calls related to today's boil water notice for Districts 3 and 4. CBECC Director Patricia Escamilla-Voss urges residents with water safety questions to call the newly established NuecesInfoLine at 361-826-INFO rather than 911. '911 is for life-threatening emergencies only,' Director Escamilla-Voss said. 'The NuecesInfoLine has operators available to answer your questions about the boil water notice, water distribution sites, and when water service is expected to be restored — please use that number and keep 911 available for people whose lives are in danger.' The NuecesInfoLine is staffed 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Information is also available in Spanish by pressing 2. Water distribution sites are open at the Tuloso-Midway High School gym, the Woodlawn Community Center, and Cefe Valenzuela Park; hours and addresses are listed at the City of Corpus Christi emergency management website.

The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center today reported that Hurricane Rafael emergency call volume has returned to near-normal levels, with 380 calls received yesterday — approaching the pre-storm daily baseline of 310 calls. CBECC Director Patricia Escamilla-Voss said the center is beginning a transition back to normal staffing over the next two weeks. 'Our dispatchers have shown extraordinary dedication over the past four weeks. The scale and duration of this response was unprecedented for our center, and I am incredibly proud of every person who answered calls, coordinated rescues, and kept working through the most demanding conditions I have seen in my career.' Director Escamilla-Voss noted that CBECC handled more than 44,200 calls in the four weeks after landfall, about five times the normal volume. The center is retaining all call records and audio as part of its standard after-action review process. Mutual aid units from San Patricio and Bee County will begin scaling back their support beginning October 14.

The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center today formally closed its Hurricane Rafael surge response posture and returned to standard staffing levels. Director Patricia Escamilla-Voss announced that CBECC has established a partnership with Nueces County Information Technology to preserve the call record archive from landfall through October 29 for training and after-action analysis purposes. The archive covers more than 56,000 calls in English and Spanish and represents the most complete 911 call record ever retained for a Gulf Coast storm response. Director Escamilla-Voss also announced a new 911 abuse reporting tip line, 1-800-NUECES-9, for residents to report suspected false emergency reports. 'During any major emergency, bad actors sometimes attempt to abuse the emergency communications system to divert rescuers,' said Escamilla-Voss. 'We take this seriously, and we ask the public to help us protect the integrity of 911 by reporting suspected abuse.' The NuecesInfoLine, opened during the boil-water notices, will close on Friday, November 5. CBECC thanks the residents of Districts 3 and 4 for their patience during the extended water notices.

news_arcs.name: The longest shift
news_arcs.description: Human-interest and operational coverage of CBECC and its dispatchers through the storm surge. Tracks the record call volume, the mutual aid operation, the boil water spike, and the gradual return to normal. Emphasizes the Spanish-language dimension of the response.

answer_key_path: The detection chain begins with the CBECC CAD incident records for D+7 through D+10, which contain 23 incidents closed as 'unfounded — no emergency found.' A metadata analyst filtering the CAD export for all unfounded incidents in this 4-day window (a low base rate — 0.3% of calls in the pre-storm corpus) will identify 23 unfounded incidents against a statistical expectation of 3–4, flagging an anomaly. Geographic mapping of the 23 incident addresses reveals a bimodal cluster around 27.802°N 97.396°W and 27.789°N 97.378°W — coordinates that fall within 400m of GW-FAC-SUB-02 and GW-FAC-SUB-03 respectively. ANI/ALI phone metadata analysis identifies all 23 originating numbers as prepaid SIMs activated within 72 hours of D+7 across three carriers — a pattern that is essentially impossible to arise from genuine resident behavior. Voice analysis of the 23 call audio files (available in the CBECC corpus) reveals average words-per-sentence of 11.3 versus 6.8 for the authentic distress call corpus, zero background noise signatures, and syntactically identical templates across English and Spanish variants — consistent with machine-generated or scripted calls. Cross-referencing the two substation coordinates with the FEMA Phase 2 aerial survey report (EVT-1106, EVT-1107) and the T8 SCADA manipulation timeline confirms that the false calls were geographically targeted at the two substations where adversary action was underway, corroborating that the disinformation and dispatch disruption were coordinated components of the same operational plan (T10).
